title: The four seasons
hook: solstices and equinoxes as your year's hinges; after the flood, God promises seedtime and harvest before the rainbow appears
tomorrow: a king's throne rose into the sky, and people named the day. what?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: retreat day. Jesus took his friends apart to rest, and met the crowd with compassion. Today the calendar widens to the whole year.

The rainbow is the famous ending of Noah's story. But read the end of Genesis 8 and something comes first. Noah steps out of the ark onto a washed-out world. He builds an altar. And before any bow appears in any cloud, God makes quieter promises: never again to smite every living thing, and one about the calendar.
screen: `THE RAINBOW, RIGHT?` → `NOAH STEPS OUT OF THE ARK.` → `A QUIETER PROMISE COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease." The puzzle is why a promise after a disaster would be about seasons. Read it from inside the ark. The flood was the year coming apart: rain that wouldn't stop, no planting, no harvest, summer and winter lost under the water. So the first gift is the year's hinges back on their pins. Spring will open, summer will burn, harvest will come in, winter will close, again and again. That's the teaching: in the Bible, the turning year isn't only weather. It's a promise God keeps. And Israel's feasts hang on that turning. Exodus says: "Three times thou shalt keep a feast unto me in the year": unleavened bread in the spring month, the feast of harvest, and the feast of ingathering at the year's end. Jewish families still keep that rhythm in Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. Your four hinges, the two solstices and the two equinoxes, can be marked in that spirit: not just dates on a calendar, but the year turning on time, the way Genesis promised. Mark them, and the year has doors you can walk through on purpose.
screen: `SEEDTIME AND HARVEST SHALL NOT CEASE.` · `THE YEAR'S HINGES BACK ON THEIR PINS.` · `THREE FEASTS ON THE TURNING YEAR.` · `SOLSTICES AND EQUINOXES AS DOORS.` · then, large: `FOUR HINGES.`

segments.voice: Look up this year's solstices and equinoxes and mark all four in your calendar. Then say the promise out loud, slowly, once: seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night. Let the last words settle before you move.
The four seasons: the year's four hinges, the solstices and equinoxes, marked the way Genesis reads the turning year, as a promise.
Take this with you: four hinges. Seedtime and harvest shall not cease. Another day in the book.

howItsDone: Jewish families keep the three pilgrim feasts on the farming year: Passover in spring, Shavuot at the wheat harvest, Sukkot at the autumn ingathering. People building their own year often mark the solstices and equinoxes with a walk, a meal or a short reading.

Noah.meaning: the man who built the ark in Genesis

Passover.meaning: the spring feast remembering the exodus from Egypt

Shavuot.meaning: the feast of weeks, at the wheat harvest

Sukkot.meaning: the autumn feast of booths, at the ingathering

equinoxes.meaning: the two days a year when day and night are about equal
